outcomes.original: Filing step: Attend the Planning Commission hearing and respond to any questions about the outdoor area location, hours, noise, and the prior 2010 withdrawal. What to say: At the hearing, present the concept as a continuation and modest enlargement of a neighborhood-serving restaurant, not a new bar. Explain that the outdoor seating is for diners waiting for tables or finishing meals, that hours will end at 10 pm, that you will monitor the sidewalk daily within a block, and that a community liaison will be available. If Commissioners or neighbors raise the 2010 withdrawal, acknowledge it and explain what is different now (for example, updated site plan, earlier closing hour, stronger operating plan, or change in ownership). If the Commission approves the CUA with conditions, accept them; the authorization is valid for three years and a building permit must be issued within that time.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register your San Francisco business and obtain a Business Account Number (BAN) from the Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector if not already registered. What to say: Register online at sftreasurer.org or in person at City Hall Room 140. The registration fee is tiered by gross receipts (for example $55 up to $100k, $95 up to $250k, $625 at $1–1.5M for 2026–27, each plus a $4 state fee). Provide your EIN and legal entity documents. The BAN is required for every other city permit (health, building, sign, ABC referral) so obtain it immediately after entity formation.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit a Public Health plan check application for the enlarged kitchen and seating area to the SF Department of Public Health Environmental Health Branch. What to say: Apply online through the DPH portal with your BAN, Location ID (LIN) and federal EIN. Submit two sets of scaled drawings showing the kitchen layout, equipment (including the hood and grease interceptor), finishes, three-compartment sink, hand sinks, and outdoor seating area, plus a menu describing food preparation. The 2026–27 flat fees are $828 (small remodel, 3 hrs), $1,241 (bar/prepackaged, 4.5 hrs), $2,207 (new restaurant, 8 hrs), with extra review at $276/hour. DPH will route the plans to Planning for zoning review. Schedule a pre-final inspection at ~80% complete and a final inspection at least two weeks before opening; both must be booked with your plan reviewer.
outcomes.note: Record confirms fees and inspection timing but does not describe the online portal, specific drawing requirements, routing to Planning, or that final inspection is two weeks before opening.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File a building permit application with the SF Department of Building Inspection for tenant improvements (kitchen build-out, seating, outdoor area construction). What to say: Submit plans stamped by a California-licensed architect showing the kitchen hood, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, ADA compliance, and outdoor seating construction. The application will be routed to Planning for zoning review under Planning Code § 175 and to DPH for health plan check. Fees are a percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–$15,000. Separate electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are pulled by licensed subcontractors. Do not start construction before the permit is issued; inspections are required at rough, final and certificate-of-occupancy stages.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Install a grease interceptor and register with the SF Public Utilities Commission Fats, Oils & Grease (FOG) program before the final building inspection. What to say: SFPUC inspectors will assign a Discharger Category (1–3) based on your cooking volume and require a grease-capturing device (trap or interceptor) sized accordingly. Install the device per the approved building plans and submit the Installation Verification Form to SFPUC; this earns a 14.2% reduction on the sewer portion of your utility bill. An undersized or missing interceptor is a common reason DBI withholds final sign-off, so coordinate with your plumber and the SFPUC inspector early.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a Health Permit to Operate after the DPH final inspection confirms the facility matches the approved plans and a certified food safety manager is on staff. What to say: Apply online at least one month before opening with your BAN, LIN and EIN. The FY2026–27 fee is $470 for the Permit to Operate application (includes initial inspection) and $0 annual license fee for restaurants and bars for 2026–28. Schedule the final inspection when construction is complete, the hood is installed and the equipment is in place. At the inspection, have proof that at least one owner or employee holds a California Food Protection Manager certificate (valid 5 years) and that all food-handling employees have Food Handler Cards (valid 3 years). The permit is issued after the inspection passes; you cannot serve the public before it is issued.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Notify ABC of the premises change and outdoor service area if required by the Type 41 license conditions, and post the required public notice. What to say: Check with ABC District Office (San Francisco) whether the enlargement and outdoor seating require a license modification or just a notification. ABC will investigate the application and may refer it to Planning and Police for review. Post the ABC public notice at the premises for 30 days as required by Business and Professions Code § 23985. If ABC refers the license to Planning, Planning will confirm that the CUA authorizes the use. Budget 60–120 days for ABC review if a modification is needed.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,100 to $15,000. Notes: The day and cost ranges cover the Conditional Use Authorization, ABC license review (if a modification is needed), and the Health permit to operate, which are the approvals in the entitlement path. The 120–300 day range is the time to approval when those approvals are granted, measured from filing the CUA to Commission approval (comparable outdoor CUAs in NCT districts took 7–268 days for approved cases, N=6), plus ABC review if triggered (60–120 days per the catalog), plus health permit processing (14–45 days per the catalog). The cost range of $3,100–$15,000 is the CUA application fee, which varies with construction cost; the 2023–24 base CUA fee was approximately $2,747 and is CPI-adjusted annually to roughly $3,150 in 2026–27, rising to $15,000 when paired with significant tenant improvements. ABC Type 41 fees ($1,000–$1,600) and health permit fees ($470 application plus $828–$2,207 plan check) are not included because the ABC license is already held (so no new license fee, though a modification may cost less than a new license) and health/building permits are needed regardless of the CUA outcome. Building permit, plan check, and construction costs are excluded because they depend on the scope of tenant improvements, not the CUA itself. The ranges assume approval; they are not times or costs to a denial or a withdrawal.
